keyPoints: ["Greater variety of species gives an ecosystem more ways to keep functioning after a loss or change.","A wider mix of ecological roles (producers, consumers, decomposers) keeps energy flow and nutrient cycling resilient.","Example: a species-rich forest tolerates losing one species better than a species-poor one."]
modelAnswer:
Biodiversity, the variety of organisms in an ecosystem, contributes to its stability because a greater variety of species means more ways for the ecosystem to keep functioning if one species is lost or a condition changes; each organism also plays a distinct ecological role (e.g. producer, consumer, decomposer), so a wider mix of roles keeps energy flow and nutrient cycling more resilient to disturbance.

Example: A forest with many plant, insect, and animal species can better withstand the loss of a single species (e.g. one pollinator) than a forest with only a few species, because other species can still perform similar roles.

keyPoints: ["Hierarchy runs from kingdom down to species","Anchor the choice in the quoted textbook wording"]
modelAnswer: Classification is the grouping of organisms according to shared characteristics. Organisms are classified by comparing cell type, nutrition, structure and reproduction, then placing them in a hierarchy of taxa: kingdom, phylum or division, class, order, family, genus and species. Modern schemes add biochemical evidence such as rRNA sequences so the groupings reflect real relationships rather than looks alone.

keyPoints: ["Two-kingdom system: oldest; only Plantae (autotrophs, plus bacteria/fungi/algae) and Animalia (heterotrophs).","Problem: organisms like Euglena (both plant-like and animal-like) don't fit cleanly.","Five-kingdom system (Whittaker, 1967): Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.","Comparison: five-kingdom system separates by cell structure (prokaryote/eukaryote), organisation and nutrition, giving finer, more accurate grouping than the two-kingdom system."]
modelAnswer: The two-kingdom classification system is the oldest classification scheme; it grouped all living organisms into just two kingdoms, Plantae and Animalia. Kingdom Plantae included the autotrophs, and bacteria, fungi and algae were also placed here, while kingdom Animalia included organisms that depend on autotrophs or other heterotrophs for food. This system struggled with organisms like Euglena, which show both plant-like traits (chlorophyll) and animal-like traits (heterotrophic nutrition, no cell wall). The five-kingdom system, introduced by Robert Whittaker in 1967, resolved this by splitting life into five kingdoms: Monera (prokaryotes, lacking a nucleus), Protista (mostly unicellular eukaryotes such as Euglena and Amoeba), Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. Comparison: the two-kingdom system uses only two broad groups and forces prokaryotes, fungi and unicellular eukaryotes into Plantae or Animalia despite their very different cell structure and nutrition; the five-kingdom system separates organisms by cell structure (prokaryote vs eukaryote), body organisation (unicellular vs multicellular) and mode of nutrition, giving a much more accurate and detailed picture of biodiversity.

keyPoints: ["Living traits: have genetic material (RNA/DNA), reproduce (using host machinery), cause disease by infecting cells.","Non-living traits: no cellular structure/enzyme system, can be crystallised, do not respire, inert outside a host.","Because of this mix, viruses are excluded from every domain and kingdom in modern classification."]
modelAnswer: Viruses show characteristics of both living and non-living things, which is why they sit at the borderline. Their living characteristics are that they occur in many varieties, carry their own genetic material (RNA or DNA), reproduce using the host cell's machinery, and enter living cells to cause disease. Their non-living characteristics are that they lack cellular structure and an enzyme system, can be crystallised and stored in a bottle, do not respire, and behave as inert, non-living infectious particles outside a host. Because they mix both sets of characteristics, viruses are not included in any domain or kingdom under modern classification.
